The Ni–Mo/CNTox catalyst showed no deactivation after four consecutive reactions, reaffirming the excellent stability of carbon-based catalysts in hydrotreatment reactions. The presence of Co led to the production of isomers in the range of the C8-C16 (entry 9, Table 5). However, the catalysts were more selective to the green diesel range (around 70%), confirming the higher capacity for deoxygenating triglycerides and less capability to crack high molecules into small ones.

Muñoz-Arjona et al. [110] showed that Mo2C supported on CNF (Mo2C/CNF) is highly effective for HDO, first using stearic acid as a model compound and then applying the catalyst to real WCO in a trickle-bed reactor. At 350 °C, Mo2C/CNF achieved up to 87 mol.% C15–C18 hydrocarbons, predominantly through the direct HDO route, but with minimal cracking (entry 10, Table 5). Earlier work by Pham et al. [142] also demonstrated the viability of carbon support, using activated-carbon-supported nickel phosphides (Ni2P/AC) for atmospheric-pressure HDO of WCO. The authors achieved more than 85% oxygen removal and produced mainly n-alkanes in the C15–C19 range (entry 11, Table 5). Ribeiro et al. [143] investigated the conversion of WCO using a physical mixture of Co-Mo/CNT and H-ZSM-5 in continuous and discontinuous modes. A high content of aromatics was obtained with these catalysts in the reaction performed in batch (around 75% of selectivity). On the other hand, the physical mixture provided a higher selectivity in C8-C16 hydrocarbons when performed in a fixed-bed reactor (entry 12, Table 5), showing the importance of aligning catalyst properties with suitable reaction systems to maximize the selectivity in the desired products.

Based on the compilation of the main results reported in the literature, there remains significant room for the development of carbon-based catalysts, particularly those based on CNT. Important knowledge gaps persist regarding how modifications to the surface chemistry of these materials, especially the introduction of acidic functional groups through nitric acid oxidation, can influence product selectivity within the C8–C16 hydrocarbon range. Furthermore, the literature demonstrates that metal-supported carbon catalysts exhibit excellent performance in deoxygenation reactions via HDO, with Mo standing out as an effective active metal phase. Nevertheless, the promotion of cracking and isomerization reactions remains limited when carbon-based catalysts are employed. Beyond surface acidity modification, the incorporation of acidic solids (such as zeolites), either through simple physical mixtures or the formation of hybrid materials, has been scarcely explored, highlighting the need for further systematic investigations.

6. Catalytic Upgrading of Plastic Waste

In addition to lipid-based feedstocks, other second-generation sources have gained increasing attention as complementary routes to meet the growing demand for SAF. Although WCO represents an attractive low-cost and low-carbon feedstock, its limited availability is insufficient to sustain large-scale SAF production [52]. In this context, alternative feedstocks such as plastic waste emerge as promising candidates due to their high hydrocarbon content, wide availability, and the urgent need for environmentally responsible disposal pathways.

Global plastic consumption has increased significantly over recent decades, leading to a substantial rise in plastic waste generation. This growing volume places significant pressure on waste management systems and represents an environmental concern. Since 1950, approximately 6.3 billion tons of plastic have been produced worldwide, of which only about 9% has been recycled [144].

From creation to disposal, plastic has detrimental consequences on the ecosystem. Its end of life causes a number of issues, including the release of toxic gases through incineration, the formation of microplastics during degradation in the environment or in landfills, which have an impact on human and animal health, and contribute to landfill overload due to its prolonged degradation time, even though its production involves the consumption of fossil resources and the emission of GHG [14]. In this context, promoting an appropriate and sustainable end-of-life destination for plastics is crucial to minimize environmental damage and ensure long-term ecological balance.

There are several classification systems for different types of plastics, which mainly depend on the stage of the plastic life cycle considered. One of the most widely used systems is the resin identification code (RIC), designed for both the use and end-of-life phases and commonly found on consumer packaging. Developed to support recycling processes, RIC originated the ASTM D7611/D7611M-20. This system defines standardized symbols and numerical codes for six packaging plastics: polyethylene terephthalate (PET), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), low-density polyethylene (LDPE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS) (all numbered from one to six, while code seven is reserved for other polymers) [145].

Overall, plastics are distinguished by their chemical composition, with each polymer consisting of repeating monomer units. Figure 9 illustrates the RIC and the condensed molecular formula of each polymer. They are composed mainly of C and H atoms and, in some cases, heteroatoms like O and Cl. Their C–C bonds can be cleaved by hydrogenolysis reactions in the presence of hydrogen pressure, temperature, and a metal-supported catalyst [13,146]. The produced hydrocarbons can undergo cracking and isomerization reactions. In this perspective, plastics are attractive feedstocks for jet fuel production due to their chemical structure and the urgency to give a final disposition to plastic waste.

The production of aviation fuel from plastic residues is not yet consolidated as one of the technologies defined by the ASTM. However, advances regarding the development of a new technological route to convert plastics have been recently debated by the ASTM Committee D02 on Petroleum Products, Liquid Fuels and Lubricants. The proposed standard route, plastic-to-jet synthetic kerosene with aromatics (PtJ-SKA), admits that the feedstock is a waste plastic processed oil made from post-consumer waste plastic mainly composed of LDPE, HDPE, and PP [147]. Consequently, studies involving the conversion of these feedstocks have been emerging in recent years. The most widely produced industrial polymers are LDPE and HDPE, and, therefore, they are also the most commonly studied in the literature [12]. From a process point of view, their conversion could be approached by applying catalytic systems analogous to those used in the upgrading of lipid-based feedstocks to SAF, adapting reaction conditions and catalyst formulations to accommodate the polymeric nature of plastics. However, it is important to note that, while lipid conversion is mainly governed by deoxygenation pathways, the conversion of polyolefins involves hydrogenolysis at metal sites and cracking reactions over both metal and acid sites.

Different catalysts have been developed to convert plastic into liquid fuels. Noble metals such as Ru have a special role in hydrogenolysis reactions and are mostly applied in polymer reactions. Commercial Ru/C was studied by Jia et al. [148], Rorrer et al. [149], and Chen et al. [146] to convert HDPE and LDPE into liquid fuels. The results showed great performance of this catalyst, with a 99–100% conversion and selectivity of 60% in C8-C16 (entry 1, Table 6), a liquid yield of 45% (entry 2, Table 6), and selectivity of 57% in C12-C20 (entry 3, Table 6). Despite differences in the use of Ru/C, some consistent trends can be observed. Complete conversion is achieved in all cases, confirming its high activity for hydrogenolysis. However, product distribution depends strongly on reaction conditions. Higher temperatures and shorter times favor C8–C16 hydrocarbons, whereas milder conditions require longer reaction times and tend to produce heavier fractions or lower liquid yields.

Other supports beyond carbon have also been investigated to enhance the catalytic performance. Cheng et al. [150] reported a maximum liquid yield of 80.7% from LDPE using Ru/milled-ZSM-22 at 290 °C, highlighting the role of zeolitic acidity in promoting controlled chain cracking (entry 4, Table 6). Nakaji et al. [19] achieved nearly complete conversion (99%) and liquid yield in C5–C21 of 84% from LDPE using Ru/CeO2 (entry 5, Table 6). However, these high liquid yields were obtained under relatively severe conditions, requiring a long reaction time (8 h) and high hydrogen pressure (60 bar), which may limit their industrial applicability. Using Ru supported on W and Zr (Ru/WZR), Wang et al. [151] reported nearly complete LDPE conversion with significant selectivity toward C8–C16 hydrocarbons (33%) and other range fuel hydrocarbons (entry 6, Table 6).

Pt- and Ni-based catalysts have also been investigated for PE conversion. Liu et al. [97] reported 99.3% LDPE conversion using Pt/Al-MCM-48, with high selectivity toward the jet fuel range, achieving 85.9% of products in the C9–C15 fraction at 300 °C (entry 7, Table 6). The mesoporous Al-MCM-48 support with moderate acidity contributed to effective diffusion and controlled chain scission, limiting cracking to lighter alkanes. In contrast, Ni-based catalysts have been explored as lower-cost alternatives, although they often require longer reaction times or more severe conditions. Zhang et al. [152] achieved 95% HDPE conversion with 80% selectivity in the C8–C16 range using Ni–Hβ after 20 h (entry 8, Table 6). Zhao et al. [153] reported complete LDPE conversion over Ni/SiO2, with 81.2% in total liquid products in the C5–C22 range (entry 9, Table 6).

The use of zeolitic catalysts as single-component systems has also been reported. Costa et al. [154] investigated H-USY (Si/Al = 15) for HDPE conversion, achieving 60% conversion at 300 °C. The product distribution was relatively balanced between the C7–C12 (48%) and C13–C20 (50%) fractions (entry 10, Table 6). It reflects the ability of zeolites to produce a wide range of alkanes, but with limited conversion. To overcome the limitations of zeolite-only systems, combined bifunctional catalytic systems, mixing metal and acid functions, have been proposed [157,158]. Liu et al. [20] reported complete LDPE conversion using Pt/WO3/ZrO2 combined with HY, although the product distribution was shifted toward lighter hydrocarbons, with 52% selectivity in the C5–C7 range (entry 11, Table 6). Similarly, Wang et al. [155] achieved full LDPE conversion using bimetallic Pt-Ru supported on trimethylsilylated micro-mesoporous silica nanocomposite (Pt-Ru/TMSN) combined with H-β, with predominant selectivity (75.6%) toward the C4–C8 fraction (entry 12, Table 6). Although mild conditions were employed, particularly the lower H2 pressure (10 bar), the use of a bimetallic noble-metal catalyst remains a limitation from a cost perspective. Finally, Ferreira et al. [156] investigated Ru/CNTox physically mixed with H-Y zeolite (entry 13, Table 6). The catalytic system was notable for its ability to selectively produce jet fuel–range hydrocarbons under solvent-free and relatively mild conditions (325 °C, 3 h, 30 bar H2). Under these conditions, it achieves a 50% liquid yield, with approximately 80% corresponding to C8–C16 hydrocarbons. In addition, the system promotes a significant level of isomerization (iso/n = 4–9) and shows high conversion and strong robustness when processing real plastic residues. Moreover, in the same study, the use of Ru/CNTox alone was insufficient to crack heavier hydrocarbons (C17–C30) into the jet fuel range, highlighting the key role of additional acid functionality provided by the zeolite in promoting cracking and isomerization reactions.

These studies demonstrate that combined catalytic systems are of interest for polymer conversion because the separation of metal and acid functions allows improved control of hydrocracking reactions. According to these authors, acid sites promote C–C bond cleavage and the formation of olefin intermediates, while metal sites enable H2 activation and hydrogenation, limiting olefin accumulation. The balance between these functions is critical, as high acidity favors cracking reactions, whereas insufficient metal activity reduces hydrogenation efficiency. Further investigation into combining metal-supported catalysts with zeolites is needed, with particular interest in the use of CNT as support for the metallic phase alongside acidic solids.

Compared to HEFA, the catalytic upgrading of plastic waste presents additional technical and economic challenges, since HEFA is currently at a more advanced technology readiness level. Plastic conversion generally involves less uniform feedstocks and less predictable reaction pathways, which complicates process control and product selectivity. In particular, the cleavage of C–C bonds during plastic hydrocracking may produce a broad product distribution, requiring additional separation and upgrading steps [159]. The process often requires relatively high temperatures and hydrogen pressures, leading to increased energy consumption and higher operating costs. Catalyst deactivation, mainly due to coke formation, metal sintering, and the presence of additives or heteroatom-containing contaminants in real mixed-plastic waste streams, also represents an important limitation. From an economic perspective, the demand for high-pressure hydrogen, the dependence on noble metal catalysts, feedstock pretreatment requirements, and the costs associated with product separation significantly affect process viability [160]. These challenges highlight the need for more selective and robust catalytic systems, improved heat management, and integrated process designs to enable large-scale production of plastic-derived SAF.

Although the addressed processes show promising performance at the laboratory scale, their scale-up remains challenging and depends strongly on reactor configuration. High hydrogen pressures and long reaction times increase operational complexity and raise safety concerns. In addition, the overall energy demand can be very high due to heating, cooling, and hydrogen compression and recycling, which significantly affect process efficiency. The need to separate and recompress unreacted hydrogen, together with broad product distributions, further increases process costs [160]. These aspects highlight that, beyond catalyst performance, process integration and energy efficiency remain critical limitations for large-scale implementation.

7. Conclusions and Future Perspectives

This work summarizes recent advances in the conversion of lipid feedstocks and plastic waste into the jet fuel range. Particular attention was given to hydroprocessing reactions, including deoxygenation, cracking, and isomerization, and the design of bifunctional heterogeneous catalysts capable of producing C8–C16 hydrocarbons, particularly highlighting the potential of carbon materials as supports.

In general, non-noble transition metals have shown a strong tendency to promote the deoxygenation pathway via HDO. In studies involving model compounds derived from lipid sources, catalysts supported on zeolites have demonstrated excellent deoxygenation and isomerization capabilities. However, several studies have reported limited catalyst stability due to coke deposition on the active sites of the zeolite pores. In contrast, carbon-based materials such as AC and CNT have been employed as catalyst supports, showing high catalytic performance and improved stability in consecutive reaction cycles. Nevertheless, these materials generally exhibit a lower intrinsic capacity for cracking and isomerization reactions. A similar trend has been observed in the catalytic conversion of vegetable oils and WCO, where mesoporous carbon-based materials such as CNT and CNF, as well as other mesostructured supports including metal oxides and mesoporous silicas, have been explored. In addition, the combination of supported catalysts with solid materials presenting moderate to high acidity has recently attracted attention, particularly for the catalytic upgrading of polyolefins into jet-fuel-range hydrocarbons. However, unlike lipid-derived feedstocks, the conversion of plastic polymers frequently relies on the use of noble metals due to the hydrogenolysis reactions required for C–C bond cleavage in polymer chains. In this context, developing non-noble transition metal catalysts with sufficient hydrogenolysis activity to replace noble metals remains a key challenge, particularly under milder hydrogen pressures and with complex plastic feedstocks.

Overall, the catalytic systems used for the conversion of lipid-based feedstocks share several similarities with those employed for upgrading plastic waste into liquid fuels, including jet fuel. This parallel suggests promising opportunities for the development of hybrid catalytic systems, such as composite materials or physical mixtures, that combine mesoporous carbon-based supports (e.g., CNT and CNF) with solids of moderate acidity, including alumina, mesoporous silicas, and moderately acidic zeolites. In particular, controlling the proportion of carbon-based materials and acid components is critical, as higher fractions of acid supports favor cracking and isomerization, whereas higher carbon content enhances metal dispersion and catalyst stability.

Exploring strategies for in situ hydrogen production could prove useful in reducing the external demand for hydrogen, although most current studies still face limitations in terms of conversion efficiency and selectivity. In particular, achieving high C8–C16 selectivity at reduced hydrogen pressures (lower than 30 bar) remains a critical target for improving process viability. The design of such multifunctional catalytic systems may contribute to improving hydrocarbon selectivity, catalyst stability, and process efficiency, ultimately supporting the large-scale production of SAF from oils and improving technologies to convert plastic residues into jet fuel.

Alaska Airlines recently reorganized its global network by successfully completing its merger with Hawaiian Airlines.

In this situation, Alaska Airlines' route serves as a stable and attractive alternative for travelers.
text:
A new wind is blowing on the skyway from Incheon to Seattle, USA.

Alaska Airlines, which has been reborn as a global network airline by taking off the long-standing label of an airline in the western United States and expanding international flights and reorganizing services, is the main character. Alaska Airlines is preparing to emerge as a new powerhouse by expanding into the Asian market through a merger with Hawaiian Airlines.

Alaska Airlines may still be somewhat unfamiliar in the Korean market.

Alaska Air Group is a global aviation group whose subsidiaries include Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, Horizon Airlines, and McGee Air Services.

It is operating at more than 140 destinations in North America, Central America, Asia and the Pacific, with major U.S. bases such as Seattle, Honolulu, Portland, Anchorage, Los Angeles, San Diego, and San Francisco as hubs.

Alaska Airlines recently reorganized its global network by successfully completing its merger with Hawaiian Airlines. As a result, the Incheon-Honolulu route, which was operated by Hawaiian Airlines, was temporarily suspended, and the Incheon-Seattle route was newly launched five times a week, enhancing access to the Americas.

It is also an official member of the global aviation alliance One World, which includes Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, and American Airlines.

Alaska Airlines is also focusing on reforming premium in-flight services in line with the expansion of international routes. The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which will be deployed on the Incheon route, is focusing on providing passengers with a more comfortable flight experience by introducing a new business suite.

Travel Plus met with Alex Jerson, executive director of Alaska Airlines Partnership and International Airlines, at the Alaska Airlines headquarters in Seattle to hear more. He joined Alaska Airlines in 2018 and served as lounge development manager, general director of alliances and partnerships. The following is the question and answer.

Q. As Alaska Airlines has launched international flights relatively recently, there are concerns that it will be somewhat lacking in operational and service know-how compared to competitors who have operated existing Incheon-Seattle routes for a long time.

In the market, Alaska Airlines can be recognized as a new airline for long-distance international flights, but we already have sufficient experience and expertise. In particular, through the recent merger with Hawaiian Airlines, it has successfully combined its long-established operational know-how in major markets such as Korea, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.

It has laid the foundation for a stable route expansion by actively utilizing Hawaiian Airlines' long experience and expertise in international flights.

In particular, the Korean team has a long career, and Yoo Soo-jin, general manager of the Asian headquarters, has also been in the group for more than a decade, gaining abundant industry experience and expertise. Based on this strong regional expertise, we will continue our successful international flights.

Q. What is the background behind the expansion of European routes despite recent geopolitical uncertainties.

Despite several volatility in the current market, demand for travel remains solid. Many travelers are continuously pursuing connections with others and new experiences, especially in major regions such as Europe and Asia.

Recent conflicts in the Middle East have restricted some of the use of major hubs by partner Qatar Airways, increasing demand for new routes to replace them. In this situation, Alaska Airlines' route serves as a stable and attractive alternative for travelers.

In addition, interest in traveling to Europe is very high among members of our loyalty program. There is a positive response to the news of the expansion of new long-distance routes such as Rome, Italy, London, England, and Reykjavik, Iceland, and positive synergy occurs, such as actively utilizing the route to establish a travel plan.

Q. Is the demand for Korean tourists increasing.

It is showing meaningful growth. Of course, it took time to reach this achievement. In the past, demand for honeymoon and leisure travel was dominated by Hawaiian Airlines, but there have been some changes since the launch of the Seattle route.

Raising awareness of Alaska Airlines' extensive network connecting to various destinations, including Seattle, was an important task. Accordingly, we have been strengthening cooperation with travel agencies and industry partners along with continuous communication, and as a result, it was confirmed that the demand for travelers departing from Korea gradually increased.

Q. Do you have a service plan tailored to the Korean market.

Customized service is one of the things Alaska Airlines is proud of. In terms of in-flight service, red pepper paste is provided together for in-flight meals, and efforts are being made to introduce local brands. In the process of composing the menu, we are also collaborating with local chefs based in Seoul.

The Incheon route will have flight attendants who can speak Korean. In addition, customer support is also being strengthened through the operation of local call centers in Seoul. In addition, Starlink Wi-Fi will be introduced sequentially on Boeing 787-9 models by the end of this year, and Korean service will be provided when subscribing to the Atmos Rewards program for free use.

Q. Sustainability is a very important factor in the airline industry today. What kind of effort is Alaska Airlines making.

There are two main tasks that are currently being focused on. First, it is promoting joint procurement of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) with One World-affiliated airlines.

Currently, a shortage of SAF supply is considered the biggest challenge, and failure to secure sufficient supplies could make it difficult to achieve environmental and sustainability goals. Accordingly, we intend to contribute to the achievement of industry-wide goals by expanding the scale of procurement and increasing supply stability through cooperation with various airlines.

The second is the side of the stylobate. The Boeing 787-9 model, which is being used on the Incheon route, is a fuel-efficient model among existing aircraft and plays an important role in reducing carbon emissions during the operation process. Through this, efforts are being made to minimize the carbon footprint throughout the flight.

Q. What are Alaska Airlines' main goals for this year.

Alaska Airlines is focused on expanding its network around two hubs, Seattle and Honolulu. Honolulu has a core market that has been operating stably for a long time, and Seattle is seeking to expand into new markets.

At the same time, it is focusing on introducing new international in-flight services and implementing them throughout the customer experience.

In addition, the most important task in the process of expanding to a new location is to effectively promote the Alaska Airlines brand itself. Markets that have entered relatively recently, such as Seoul and Tokyo, are also focusing on raising brand awareness.

This year, it plans to actively promote its brand while focusing on growing the market stably and expanding demand. With the recent completion of Hawaiian Airlines' membership in One World, synergy at the level of aviation alliances has also been strengthened.

With such various strategies and changes in parallel, expectations are high for changes and growth in the future, with the upcoming summer season and Starlink service scheduled to be introduced by the end of this year. It is expected to be an important turning point in providing customers with a further improved service experience along with the expansion of international networks.

title: Barbados Joins Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Dominica, Antigua & Barbuda, Saint ... - Travel And Tour World
description:
• Middle East fuel supply disruptions in 2026 have driven jet fuel price volatility.
Impact of Middle East Energy Disruptions on Caribbean Aviation Fuel Costs The Middle East energy crisis of 2026 has had a profound impact on global aviation, including the Caribbean.
A Greener, More Resilient Caribbean Aviation Future Barbados, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Dominica, Antigua & Barbuda, and Saint Vincent & the Grenadines are leading the charge towards a greener, more resilient aviation industry by prioritizing Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) adoption in 2026.
In conclusion, Barbados, alongside Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Dominica, Antigua & Barbuda, Saint Vincent and others in groundbreaking sustainable aviation initiatives to address the jet fuel crisis.
These strategic actions aim to lower airline costs, boost Caribbean tourism, and transform the travel experience.
text:
Barbados joins Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Dominica, Antigua & Barbuda, Saint Vincent and others in groundbreaking sustainable aviation initiatives to tackle the jet fuel crisis and these efforts aim to lower airline costs, boost Caribbean tourism, and transform the travel experience amid ongoing Middle East energy disruptions.

In response to the mounting challenges of the jet fuel crisis and global energy disruptions, a coalition of Caribbean nations including Barbados, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Dominica, Antigua & Barbuda, and Saint Vincent are pioneering a collective movement towards Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) initiatives. These nations aim to lower airline operational costs, mitigate carbon emissions, and bolster the tourism sector amid the ongoing geopolitical upheavals from the Middle East energy crisis. This regional collaboration promises to not only provide a viable solution to fuel shortages but also reshape the Caribbean’s aviation landscape, positioning the region as a leader in sustainability and eco-friendly travel.

Caribbean Aviation Faces Historic Shift to Sustainable Aviation Fuel in 2026

The Caribbean’s aviation industry is undergoing a historic shift in 2026 as Barbados, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Dominica, Antigua & Barbuda, and Saint Vincent & the Grenadines move toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) adoption in response to unprecedented jet fuel market volatility driven by Middle East energy disruptions. SAF represents a renewable, cleaner alternative to conventional jet kerosene certified to reduce lifecycle CO₂ emissions by up to 80% on a well‑to‑wake basis, a key pillar of ICAO’s global emissions reduction framework. Global SAF production remains nascent, covering less than 1% of jet fuel demand in 2026, yet accelerating geopolitical pressures and cost spikes from jet fuel supply bottlenecks have propelled Caribbean stakeholders to prioritize SAF feasibility and regulatory alignment. The region’s tourism‑dependent economies are now linking aviation decarbonization directly to energy security, cost stabilization, and brand positioning for sustainable travel.

• SAF can cut aviation CO₂ emissions by up to ~80% compared with traditional jet fuel.

• Global SAF output is projected to reach ~2.4 Mt in 2026, covering less than 1% of total jet fuel use.

• Middle East fuel supply disruptions in 2026 have driven jet fuel price volatility.

• ICAO’s Global Framework supports SAF deployment and policy planning.

• Caribbean tourism and airline stability are key drivers of SAF interest.

Barbados Elevates National SAF Strategy to Secure Tourism and Cut Fuel Costs

Barbados has formally integrated SAF considerations into its aviation and energy policy frameworks in 2026 to mitigate escalating jet fuel costs triggered by global supply constraints and Middle East geopolitical tensions. While detailed local SAF production figures are not yet public, national policymakers are collaborating with ICAO’s ACT‑SAF assistance programmes to evaluate feedstock viability, investment pathways, and infrastructure readiness. Barbados’ strategy blends renewable feedstock assessments with regional cooperation efforts to attract public‑private capital for future SAF synthesis facilities. In practical terms, SAF deployment is being positioned to lower dependency on imported fossil jet fuel, which historically makes up nearly all aviation energy demand — a vulnerability exposed by 2026’s historically high jet fuel price volatility stemming from disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

• Barbados is evaluating SAF feasibility with ICAO support.

• National focus tied to tourism cost competitiveness.

• Jet fuel import reliance creates economic volatility.

• Potential feedstocks include waste oils and biomass processing.

• Integration seeks to reduce carbon footprint and energy imports.

Jamaica Champions Regional SAF Drive to Stabilize Fuel Costs and Grow Tourism

Jamaica in 2026 has positioned Sustainable Aviation Fuel as a national priority to stabilize airline operational costs and bolster competitiveness in international tourism markets. Jamaican civil aviation authorities are assessing SAF feedstock potential and regulatory pathways aligned with ICAO’s global SAF deployment standards. While Caribbean nations are at varying stages, Jamaica’s engagement underscores the urgency brought on by global jet fuel supply instability and rising costs, which have repeatedly forced airlines globally to raise fares and reroute flights. The island’s strategy places SAF both as a decarbonization mechanism and a cost‑risk hedge, with economic projections linking enhanced fuel security to incremental tourism inflows and job creation in energy and transport sectors.

• Jamaica aligns SAF planning with international frameworks.

• Jet fuel price volatility threatens tourism demand.

• SAF seen as strategic energy risk mitigation.

• Feedstock evaluation linked to local agricultural outputs.

• Expected to enhance airline competitiveness.

Saint Lucia Advances SAF Awareness to Boost Eco‑Tourism and Travel Resilience

In 2026 Saint Lucia’s aviation and tourism stakeholders are increasingly prioritizing Sustainable Aviation Fuel as part of broader resilience planning. Although formal SAF production plans have yet to be published, the national government is incorporating SAF discussions into renewable energy strategy frameworks, tourism development plans, and climate resilience commitments referenced in regional dialogues. title: Airlines in Europe Brace for Jet Fuel Shortage Amid Safety Concerns - Travel And Tour World
description:
Europe’s airlines are bracing for a significant jet fuel supply challenge that could reshape how flights operate through 2026.
The warning comes as oil and jet fuel supply chains face pressure due to conflict‑related disruptions near key energy export routes.
What Is Causing the Jet Fuel Pressure on Airlines?
Geopolitical Strains Jet fuel supplies throughout Europe are influenced heavily by global petrochemical markets and refining infrastructure.
SAF are aviation fuels derived from renewable feedstocks—such as waste oils, recycled carbon fuels, and synthetic aviation fuels—designed to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions.
text:
Europe’s airlines are bracing for a significant jet fuel supply challenge that could reshape how flights operate through 2026. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has issued urgent safety guidance about shifting from the standard European Jet A‑1 aviation fuel to the U.S.‑standard Jet A grade to prevent looming supply disruptions as geopolitical tensions intensify in the Middle East.

The warning comes as oil and jet fuel supply chains face pressure due to conflict‑related disruptions near key energy export routes. Although Europe currently has sufficient reserves, regulators are preparing for scenarios where traditional fuel sources could tighten, especially during peak summer travel demand.

What Is Causing the Jet Fuel Pressure on Airlines? Geopolitical Strains

Jet fuel supplies throughout Europe are influenced heavily by global petrochemical markets and refining infrastructure. The ongoing conflict involving Iran has created uncertainties for fuel shipments from the Middle East—a historically critical supplier region—raising concerns that Europe may face strained aviation fuel pipelines if tensions persist.

European officials acknowledge that traditional Jet A‑1 fuel, used widely due to its low freezing point and certification for long‑haul flight operations, could see limited availability if shipping bottlenecks worsen. This has led to coordination with international partners, including the United States, to import Jet A fuel as a contingency and ensure flights can continue uninterrupted.

EASA Safety Guidance — What Airlines Must Know About Jet A Fuel

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has formally issued a Safety Information Bulletin instructing airlines and airports on how to safely manage the use of Jet A fuel within European markets traditionally reliant on Jet A‑1.

This guidance highlights differences in freezing point and handling procedures between the two fuel grades, underscoring the need for careful planning and communication throughout the fuel supply chain. Crew training, updated fuel documentation, and operational checks are part of compliance protocols that airlines must follow to maintain passenger safety standards.

Critically, regulators confirm there are no legal obstacles preventing the use of Jet A fuel in Europe when applied with proper safety measures. This flexibility aims to help carriers avoid supply shortages without compromising operational rules.

EU ReFuelEU Regulation Drives Long‑Term Aviation Fuel Strategy

Beyond immediate supply concerns, the European Commission’s ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation establishes a long‑term plan to transition the industry toward Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF). Under this official EU regulation, minimum shares of SAF blended into jet fuel delivered to EU airports begin at 2% in 2025 and rise significantly through 2050.

SAF are aviation fuels derived from renewable feedstocks—such as waste oils, recycled carbon fuels, and synthetic aviation fuels—designed to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions. This mandate is part of the EU’s Fit for 55 climate strategy to cut greenhouse gas emissions from aviation and transport.

Europe may have even exceeded its 2% SAF target in 2025, indicating initial success in early adoption. However, SAF production capacity remains limited and more costly than conventional fuels, posing supply and economic challenges for airlines and fuel suppliers.

SAF — The Sustainable Alternative That Also Strengthens Fuel Security

Sustainable Aviation Fuels are not just a green policy; they represent a strategic buffer in energy supply diversification. SAF can be produced from a variety of sources that do not depend on volatile oil markets, including bio‑derived substances and next‑generation synthetic fuels made from renewable energy and captured carbon.

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) recognises SAF as a key tool to cut CO₂ emissions from international aviation by up to 5% by 2030, and much more by mid‑century if adoption accelerates.

European regulators are betting on expanding SAF supply chains to reduce fossil dependence and increase resilience against supply shocks. Initiatives are underway to boost production facilities in the EU and foster global partnerships with innovative fuel producers.

Why This Matters for Travellers and Flight Operations

For millions of travellers planning flights this summer and beyond, the jet fuel situation could influence travel costs and airline operations. Although regulators stress that fuel supply remains adequate for now, airlines may adjust schedules, reconfigure routes, or raise airfares to cope with fuel procurement and handling complexities.

Importantly, EU authorities emphasise that passenger rights remain protected under current law, and airlines must observe compensation rules even if fuel price pressures impact flight performance. Scheduled cancellations due solely to economic pressure do not qualify for exemption from passenger rights protections.

Balancing Safety, Sustainability, and Travel Demand

Regulators and airline stakeholders are navigating a challenging era where energy security, environmental responsibility, and economic realities collide. EASA’s real‑time safety guidance represents a flexible operational response to immediate supply risks, while the ReFuelEU framework charts a structural shift toward greener fuel use over the next decade.

For travellers and industry watchers alike, the aviation sector’s ability to manage both fuel diversity and sustainability commitments will play a defining role in shaping flight availability, pricing, and environmental impact through the coming years.

title: PRC Europe 2026: how oil and gas is adapting to net zero - Offshore Technology
description:
PRC Europe 2026 will take place in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, from 18–19 May.
ReFuelEU Aviation already requires fuel suppliers to raise the share of sustainable aviation fuel at EU airports, starting at 2% from 2025 and increasing over time.
How the industry is responding – discussions ahead of PRC Europe 2026 The downstream sector is testing potential ways to repurpose existing assets, rather than waiting on a new infrastructure base to emerge.
Rocio Gil Bosque, aviation market development manager at Repsol Fuels, will speak on regulatory and technological challenges for large-scale SAF manufacturing at PRC Europe.
Co-processing, SAF scale-up and refinery flexibility are different responses to the same underlying pressure, and the foundation of conversations for PRC Europe.
text:
PRC Europe 2026 will take place in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, from 18–19 May. Delegates are set to discuss the future-proofing of downstream operations, as pressure builds around emissions targets. As operators look to adapt existing assets, protect competitiveness and build lower-carbon product portfolios, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel are becoming central to long-term strategy.

Refining is being forced to change

Refining is being pushed into a different operating logic. The old model was built around conventional fuel output, utilisation rates and margin management. However, it is experiencing converging pressures.

In Europe, that pressure is regulatory and structural: the EU Climate Law outlines the bloc’s path towards climate neutrality by 2050, and specifies 55% as a minimum reduction target for net greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Simultaneously, new regulation around transport is starting to reshape demand and scale for cleaner fuels.

That matters directly for refineries. ReFuelEU Aviation already requires fuel suppliers to raise the share of sustainable aviation fuel at EU airports, starting at 2% from 2025 and increasing over time. Meanwhile, the EU’s tighter CO₂ standards for cars and vans are designed around a 100% emissions-reduction target for new vehicles from 2035.

Concurrently, the International Energy Agency expects global oil demand growth to slow towards 2030. It also expects global road transport fuel demand to peak in 2028, with earlier peaks forecast in Europe and the US. Refiners are therefore facing two substantial shifts: stronger demand-side pressure for lower-carbon fuels and weaker long-term growth prospects for parts of the traditional road-fuel pool. The industry must respond while working alongside existing refinery systems.

How the industry is responding – discussions ahead of PRC Europe 2026

The downstream sector is testing potential ways to repurpose existing assets, rather than waiting on a new infrastructure base to emerge. The shape of the sector’s next chapter is gradually emerging, becoming apparent through a mix of technology choices, feedstock strategies, hydrogen pathways and project models designed to make lower-carbon fuels more viable at scale. PRC Europe 2026 will reflect that shift by bringing together senior voices from engineering, infrastructure, licensing, petrochemicals, procurement and construction, refining and technology to discuss the routes the industry is actively evaluating now.

Co-processing of renewable feedstocks

One of the clearest examples is co-processing, which shows how operators are trying to adapt existing refinery units, rather than relying entirely on new-build solutions. Henrik Rådberg, head of new opportunities at VAROPreem, will address this topic at the conference, via a presentation on the co-processing of renewable feedstocks to road and aviation fuels. He notes that “co-processing is a pragmatic transition strategy”, which allows renewable feedstocks – waste oils, fats and bio-oils – to be processed with fossil intermediates in existing refinery units, making it possible to scale lower-carbon road fuels and SAF faster, and with less capital intensity than a full greenfield approach.

However, it comes with technical and regulatory demands. Rådberg highlights that feedstock flexibility only creates value when supported by robust pretreatment, fuel quality control, sustainability certification and transparent mass-balance accounting. Thus, co-processing is relevant not as a sole solution but as a practical bridge between today’s fossil refinery system and the next stage of renewable fuels development.

Overcoming challenges in SAF manufacturing

A related, but more difficult, question is scale. Rocio Gil Bosque, aviation market development manager at Repsol Fuels, will speak on regulatory and technological challenges for large-scale SAF manufacturing at PRC Europe. For the industry, conversations around SAF are shifting from refinery adaptation and production to the conditions needed to push SAF towards mainstream commercial viability.

SAF is already at the centre of aviation decarbonisation plans. However, as Bosque underlines, “fragmented policies, evolving sustainability criteria and constrained feedstock eligibility create investment uncertainty”. That uncertainty continues to slow commercial decisions.

However, SAF scaling remains inextricably tied to refinery systems. This is recognised by Repsol, which treats refining as a multi-product platform, where viability depends on balancing the full output slate, rather than maximising a single fuel stream.

Bosque explains that “refining systems operate as multi-product platforms”, which means SAF expansion has to be assessed alongside renewable road fuels, hydrogen demand, feedstock flexibility and broader production economics. That logic becomes more sharply evident in emerging pathways such as e-fuels, where large volumes of renewable hydrogen, reliable CO₂ supply and major capital commitments remain critical constraints.

Creating the refineries of the future

If co-processing shows one near-term route and SAF scale-up highlights the challenge of volume, Jose de Barros, chief decarbonisation officer at Lummus Technology (regional partner of PRC Europe 2026), will offer a wider asset-level view with his speech on sustainability and profit pathways in the energy transition era. The focus reflects a question that is becoming increasingly central to refining: what does a future-ready plant actually look like when the market is being reshaped?

When operators use decarbonisation as a way to reduce emissions, diversify feedstocks, improve efficiency and open access to new low-carbon markets, “sustainability and profitability move in the same direction”, says Barros. This is an important shift in emphasis – resilience is being treated less as an environmental slogan and more as an operational and commercial issue.

Barros also underlines that the refinery of the future will need to function as a more flexible industrial platform than the one inherited from the fossil-centric era. That means combining electrification, circularity, renewable feedstocks, hydrogen and digital optimisation in ways that reinforce each other. In his words, assets need to evolve into “flexible platforms capable of processing circular and renewable feedstocks, producing sustainable fuels and optimising energy use through digital tools”.

Operators that reposition their plants early, and do so through partnerships across technology, recycling, digital and process innovation, will be better placed to meet future standards and remain competitive as traditional fuel demand becomes less predictable.

The next stage of downstream transformation

Taken together, these examples show that future-proofing refining is not about one fuel or one technology. Co-processing, SAF scale-up and refinery flexibility are different responses to the same underlying pressure, and the foundation of conversations for PRC Europe. The Congress attracts oil and gas leaders across the value chain and places decarbonisation, low-carbon feedstock, hydrogen potential, project execution and investment readiness in one connected discussion.

Egypt Positions Suez Canal Zone For Cleaner Aviation Fuel

Green Sky Capital has signed financing for a sustainable fuel facility in Egypt’s Suez Canal Economic Zone, placing the country closer to a fast-growing but still constrained market for lower-carbon transport fuels.

The facility is expected to produce up to 200,000 tons of biofuels a year. Its planned product slate includes sustainable aviation fuel, hydro-treated vegetable oil, bio propane and bio naphtha. For airlines, refiners and investors, the project lands at a critical point.

Aviation remains one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize. Aircraft have limited near-term options for replacing liquid fuels at scale. As a result, sustainable aviation fuel has become central to the industry’s 2050 climate pathway. Yet supply remains limited, production costs remain high, and offtake markets are still forming.

That gap is creating a major opportunity for fuel producers and infrastructure investors. It is also putting pressure on governments to build local and regional supply chains before regulation tightens further.

Gulf Capital Backs Regional Fuel Infrastructure

Green Sky Capital is a sustainable aviation fuel platform developing renewable fuel projects across the Middle East and North Africa. Its backers include sponsors with experience in infrastructure, energy and industrial development.

That mix matters. Sustainable fuel projects require more than climate ambition. They need feedstock security, industrial execution, long-term offtake, supportive policy and credible financing. Without those elements, many announced projects struggle to move from concept to production.

For Egypt, the location adds strategic weight. The Suez Canal Economic Zone sits at one of the world’s most important trade corridors. A biofuels facility there could serve regional transport demand while supporting Egypt’s wider industrial and energy-transition ambitions.

RELATED ARTICLE: Comcast Fully Allocates $1 Billion Green Bond to Sustainability Projects

Airlines Face Rising Fuel Pressure

The aviation sector’s fuel challenge is becoming more urgent. Airlines have committed to long-term decarbonization goals, but the path remains difficult. Sustainable aviation fuel is widely viewed as the most practical near-term tool for cutting lifecycle emissions from flights. However, it still accounts for only a small share of global jet fuel use.

Cost is the central obstacle. Alternative fuels are often far more expensive than conventional kerosene. Airlines already face thin margins, volatile demand cycles and rising pressure from regulators and customers. Fuel is also one of their largest single expenses.

Geopolitical shocks can intensify that pressure. The war in Iran has added concern over traditional fuel costs, giving alternative fuel investment new urgency. When kerosene prices rise, the economics of diversification become more relevant for airlines and investors.

Still, the market cannot scale on price pressure alone. Producers need long-term buyers. Airlines need reliable supply. Governments need to create policy frameworks that reward cleaner fuel use without placing unsustainable cost burdens on carriers.

What Executives And Investors Should Watch

For C-suite leaders, the Green Sky Capital project is about more than one facility. It points to a broader shift in how aviation fuel security, climate policy and industrial investment are starting to converge.

Investors will watch whether the Egypt facility can secure feedstock, meet its construction timeline and convert partnerships into long-term commercial demand. Airlines will watch pricing and availability. Policymakers will watch whether regional production can reduce dependence on imported fuels while supporting emissions goals.

The project also adds to the Middle East and North Africa’s role in the global energy transition. The region has long been central to fossil fuel markets. Now, governments and investors are trying to position parts of the region for future fuel supply chains as well.

If Green Sky Capital’s Egypt facility reaches commercial operations by the end of 2027, it could become a reference point for sustainable aviation fuel development in emerging markets. Its real test will be whether it can turn capital commitments and industrial partnerships into scalable, competitive supply.

THUNDER BAY – Greenwater Technology is receiving a $5.5 million investment from the province to support the production of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel using mill byproducts and underused wood fibre.

The investment will help Greenwater Technology convert the former wafer board facility at Thunder Bay Pulp and Paper into a commercial-scale demonstration and testing facility to refine the company’s biofuel technology.

The total project cost is expected to be approximately $15 million.

“This is the first-of-its-kind technology,” said James Irving, president of Greenwater Ltd. “Before you can get a bank loan to build the big one, you’ve got to prove that it’ll work at scale.”

Irving said the company hopes to complete construction of the demonstration facility by the end of September, before beginning extended operational testing.

“We’re trying to prove out the yield so that we can get 300 litres of fuel for every tonne of wood that we put into it,” he said.

“Thunder Bay is the perfect location to build this demonstration facility,” Irving added. “It has everything — from research support at Lakehead University, fabrication at Venshore Mechanical, design support from Nordmin Engineering, a location like Thunder Bay Pulp and Paper, and, of course, wood fibre from local forestry operations.”

Greenwater’s process will convert forest biomass into renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel more efficiently and at a lower cost than older technologies.

“The energy is in the wood,” Irving said. “The trick has always been how to get it out in a way that’s competitive with petroleum.”

Once the pilot unit is operational, it is expected to process approximately 10 tonnes of dry biomass per day and produce roughly 3,000 litres of fuel daily.

Wood chips will be fed into the front-end system before entering a reactor vessel, where the material undergoes thermocatalytic depolymerisation at approximately 290 C. Vapours produced during the process will rise from the reactor and be condensed into liquid fuel before undergoing additional refining and cleaning.

Thunder Bay-Atikokan MPP Kevin Holland said the project fits within the province’s broader strategy to modernize and diversify the forest sector through Ontario’s forestry roadmap.

“This project is an inspiring example of forest sector innovation,” Holland said. “This is an example of the adapt stage of our roadmap, where we’re finding new innovative products and diversifying what we can create using forest biomass to help replace some of what has been lost with the downturn in the industry itself."

Scott Jackson of the Centre for Research and Innovation in the Bio-Economy (CRIBE) said global demand for sustainable aviation fuel continues to grow.

“By 2030, aircraft landing in the European Union will require six per cent sustainable aviation fuel,” Jackson said, noting similar mandates are emerging in other international markets.

He added that the project could create new markets for forest byproducts while supporting jobs and economic growth across Northern Ontario.

Irving said the technology could eventually be expanded to other mill sites across Northern Ontario where stable wood supplies are available.

“Wherever we can find a long-term stable supply of affordable wood, we can set up close by and really keep the forestry ecosystem stronger in those communities,” he said.

Irving said the project also provides an opportunity for existing industrial infrastructure in Thunder Bay and in other parts of the region.

“We are revitalizing an old industrial facility and turning it into something designed for the future,” he said.

The funding includes $5 million under the Forest Biomass Program, as well as $500,000 through the Northern Ontario Heritage Fund Corporation.

title: STATEMENT: Environmental Organizations Issue Letter Opposing US Ethanol 'E15' Fuel Bill
description:

However, a growing body of scientific evidence now indicates that biofuels derived from food and feed crops probably result in higher emissions than conventional fossil fuels.
This emerging science led the European Union, which had adopted large biofuel targets, to place much lower caps on crop-based biofuels.
Contrary to claims that ethanol lowers fuel costs, production expenses for corn ethanol typically exceed those of gasoline, except during periods of unusually high oil prices—and even then, ethanol prices tend to rise in tandem with global energy markets.
EPA, “Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) Program: Standards for 2023–2025 and Other Changes, Regulatory Impact Analysis” (June 2023).
text:
WASHINGTON (May 8, 2026) — A group of environmental organizations shared the below open letter with the U.S. House of Representatives opposing proposed "year-round E15" legislation that would allow gasoline blended with 15 percent ethanol to be sold throughout the year, an increase from the common 10 percent blend.

The organizations include World Resources Institute, Sierra Club, Earthjustice Action, Waterkeeper Alliance, Mighty Earth, Clean Wisconsin, Kentucky Waterways Alliance, and Wisconsin’s Green Fire, Inc.

Letter Text:

The undersigned organizations write to express strong opposition to proposals advancing so-called “year-round E15” legislation, which would effectively override key provisions of the Clean Air Act by permitting gasoline blended with 15 percent ethanol to be sold throughout the year—an increase from the common 10 percent blend. Given prior indications of executive support for E15, which could then mandate it, enactment of this legal change would likely drive a 50% substantial expansion in ethanol use. Such a shift would require dedicating vast additional acreage to ethanol—exceeding half the size of Indiana—with serious consequences for our climate, natural resources, wildlife, and consumers.

Climate Impacts. When Congress enacted the Renewable Fuel Standard in 2007, it required that qualifying biofuels achieve reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. However, a growing body of scientific evidence now indicates that biofuels derived from food and feed crops probably result in higher emissions than conventional fossil fuels. This emerging science led the European Union, which had adopted large biofuel targets, to place much lower caps on crop-based biofuels. Similarly, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Science Advisory Board reported in 2023 that recent estimates of corn ethanol emissions exceed those of gasoline.1 Reflecting these findings, even as the EPA increased biofuel requirements at the direction of the Trump Administration, it declined to conclude that food-based biofuels reduce emissions, even when combined with additional lower-emission biofuels derived from waste.

The emissions associated with corn ethanol stem not only from fossil energy inputs during production—which offset much of its purported benefit—but also from land-use changes. As cropland expands to replace food production diverted to fuel, forests and grasslands are converted, releasing significant stores of carbon.2 Globally, converting land for corn ethanol production typically releases roughly twice the carbon saved from reduced gasoline tailpipe emissions over a 30-year period.3 These dynamics contribute to agricultural expansion, which accounts for approximately 10 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.4 In a world where agricultural yield growth is not keeping pace with rising food demands, increasing biofuels requires either increasing hunger5 or exacerbating emissions—neither of which is acceptable.

Other Environmental Consequences. Beyond climate concerns, crop-based biofuels are associated with a range of additional environmental harms. These include heightened water pollution, increased strain on limited water supplies, and the conversion of millions of acres of valuable wildlife habitat into cropland. Such impacts have been documented extensively in the scientific literature6 and acknowledged by federal agencies.7

Economic Costs and Limited Energy Benefits. The economic implications of expanding E15 are also significant. The EPA has estimated that even a more modest increase in biofuel use would impose approximately $41 billion in additional fuel and food costs over a three-year period—outweighing estimated energy security benefits 80-fold.8 These costs include an estimated $24 billion in higher fuel costs, and $17 billion in higher food prices, translating to roughly $50 annually in increased household food costs per year. Contrary to claims that ethanol lowers fuel costs, production expenses for corn ethanol typically exceed those of gasoline, except during periods of unusually high oil prices—and even then, ethanol prices tend to rise in tandem with global energy markets. At a time when American families are already confronting elevated costs, year-round E15 would impose additional burdens both at the pump and at the grocery store.

Distributional Effects. While EPA has found biofuel policies transfer billions of dollars from consumers to the agricultural sector, the benefits are unevenly distributed. Rising crop prices are quickly reflected in higher land values and rents. Over the past two decades, inflation-adjusted cropland values in states like Iowa have increased by 250%,9 in part due to biofuel demand. Because a majority of farmland in the Corn Belt is leased10—and nearly 80% of that land is owned by those who have never farmed—most of the financial gain accrues to investors rather than working farmers.11

For these reasons, we respectfully urge you to oppose efforts to expand year-round E15 and instead support more effective, sustainable approaches to energy and transportation policy. We should not commit additional land, resources, or taxpayer dollars to policies that undermine our climate goals, strain our natural systems, and increase costs for American families.

Sincerely,

World Resources Institute12

Sierra Club

Earthjustice Action

Waterkeeper Alliance

Mighty Earth

Clean Wisconsin

Kentucky Waterways Alliance

Wisconsin’s Green Fire, Inc.

Notes:

1. Letter to Michael Regan from EPA Science Advisory Board, “Commentary on the Volume Requirements for 2023 and Beyond under the Renewable Fuel Standard Program” (RIN 2060-AV14) (September 29, 2023).

2. “Environmental outcomes of the US Renewable Fuel Standard.” Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 119(9) (2022); “Choices in Land Representation Materially Affect Modeled Biofuel Carbon Intensity Estimates.” Journal of Cleaner Production 349 (May 2022): 131477.

3. “Assessing the Efficiency of Changes in Land Use for Mitigating Climate Change.” Nature 564: 249 (2018). This calculation fully credits ethanol with feed by-products.

4. “Global Carbon Budget 2021.” Earth System Science Data 14, 1917-2005 (2022).

5. The land use and biofuel model favored by the biofuel industry estimates low land use change in part because it estimates that roughly half of the calories are not replaced because higher crop prices lead to reduced food consumption. “Do Biofuel Policies Seek to Cut Emissions by Cutting Food?” Science 347:1420-22 (2015).

6. “Environmental outcomes of the US Renewable Fuel Standard.” Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 119(9) (2022); “Cropland Expansion in the United States Produces Marginal Yields at High Costs to Wildlife.” Nature Communications 11:1 (2020); “US Agricultural Policy, Land Use Change, and Biofuels: Are We Driving Our Way to the next Dust Bowl?” Environmental Research Letters 10, no. 5 (2015).

7. EPA, “Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) Program: Standards for 2023–2025 and Other Changes, Regulatory Impact Analysis” (June 2023).

8. EPA, “Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) Program: Standards for 2023–2025 and Other Changes, Regulatory Impact Analysis” (June 2023), p. 369 for estimates of food costs, p. v for estimates of energy costs, and p. vi for estimates of energy security benefits.

9. USDA, Iowa Farmland Rental Rates 1994-2025 (accessed May 4, 2026).

10. USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service's 2022 Census of Agriculture.

11. “Millions Of Acres of U.S. Farmland Rented,” Farms.com (March 13, 2026).

12. For further information, contact Janet Ranganathan, Managing Director, World Resources Institute.

title: Billions in investment waiting for biofuel policy certainty, super investors say - ABC News
description:
Billions of dollars worth of investment will flow if the federal government mandates a percentage of biofuels be added to the nation's fuel supply, major investors say.
Biofuels, made from organic matter, have been positioned as a renewable alternative to fossil fuels that could be made here, bolstering fuel supply.
Farmers ready to supply biofuel raw materials Australia currently imports 77 per cent of its refined fuel needs.
$3b super investment ready and waiting IFM is the investment manager for Australia's enormous industry superannuation funds.
Australia has a small biofuels industry, and most of the output is exported.
text:
Billions of dollars worth of investment will flow if the federal government mandates a percentage of biofuels be added to the nation's fuel supply, major investors say.

If the government makes a definitive decision on biofuels, superannuation investor Danny Elia told ABC News he could raise funds immediately to build a refinery, starting a process to lower fuel prices for Australian consumers.

"I would turn up to my investment committee tomorrow, asking for the support to invest in what would be our first plant, which would produce 8 per cent equivalent of the country's aviation fuel," the head of infrastructure assets at IFM Investors said.

Fuel security has been in the spotlight since the Middle East war sent shockwaves through global oil markets and raised questions about potential shortages in Australia.

Biofuels, made from organic matter, have been positioned as a renewable alternative to fossil fuels that could be made here, bolstering fuel supply.

On Wednesday, the prime minister announced more than $10 billion would be spent on bolstering Australia's fuel security, including expanding onshore reserves and exploring the feasibility of more local refining.

This week's announcement focused on getting and storing more crude-oil-based fuels, however last September, the government also announced $1.1 billion in grants to promote the expansion of biofuel production.

Farmers ready to supply biofuel raw materials

Australia currently imports 77 per cent of its refined fuel needs. The rest is refined here, but largely from crude oil imports.

In February, only nine barrels of every 100 used here were actually pumped out of the ground in Australia or its waters.

Agricultural groups have positioned themselves as the short and long-term solution to our fuel sovereignty problem, while building a biofuels industry that adds value to crops Australia already ships out.

"Farmers already supply products that power biofuel industries overseas," said National Farmers' Federation chief executive officer Mike Guerin.

Australia has the ingredients to make biofuels, but what has held them back is the lack of consistent demand that would allow big investments.

$3b super investment ready and waiting

IFM is the investment manager for Australia's enormous industry superannuation funds. It had $266.1 billion in funds under management at the end of last year, so Mr Elia is not kidding around.

The plant would be built next to Ampol's refinery in Lytton, a suburb of Brisbane, and be ready to go in five years.

Crop giant GrainCorp is involved as well, and is set to build a plant to crush canola for the new refinery.

It shows the potential scale of biofuels, but also demonstrates the reason Australia's biofuel industry is so small, despite having vast amounts of land, ingredients and potential.

Mr Elia said the market needed strong signals about demand to trigger the kind of long-term investment required.

If it got them, Australia could produce a billion litres of low-carbon fuel by 2030 or 2032 and "grow exponentially from there", Mr Elia said.

"If you spread that across aviation and broader transport, like diesel, probably something in the order of about 30 per cent to 40 per cent of [liquid fuel] by 2040."

Not a supply problem, a lack of demand

Biofuels like sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and biodiesel are more expensive to produce in Australia than imported fossil fuels like crude oil.

With global prices for liquid fuels currently elevated by the conflict in the Middle East, they are competitive.

But that has not always been the case, and it is not expected to persist if the situation stabilises and global crude oil prices fall.

In this scenario, locally produced fuel would become more expensive than imported products, which currently satisfy close to 80 per cent of Australia's liquid fuel needs.

Without consistent decades-long demand, the Australian industry has said it cannot expand to reach sufficient size and breadth.

Mark Brown, the chair of the International Energy Agency's Bioenergy Technology Collaboration Programme, said if investors were going to be asked to spend billions on biofuels, they needed to know they would get a return.

A so-called "demand-side" mechanism, such as a government mandate that a certain percentage of fuel must be blended with biofuels, would build that confidence among investors.

Professor Brown pointed to overseas examples as evidence.

"Where we see bioenergy or renewable fuels having success, they have been supported or underpinned by things like fuel mandates that promote blending and create those market certainties that allow the investment to flow," he said.

Calls for legislated biofuel mandates

Barbara Kiss worked for General Motors for more than 24 years, most recently as the director of emissions compliance.

Now a consultant, she has worked with ethanol producer Manildra Group, an agribusiness that manufactures food and industrial products.

She spoke to the ABC about sugarcane biofuel, which is blended with petrol and used in standard cars and light vehicles.

"In the US, the demand-side mechanism ended up being a mandate," she said.

"The federal government just said, 'We're going to do this. We're going do this across the board. It's the right thing to do for all of these reasons.'"

Now E15 — a mix of petrol and up to 15 per cent ethanol — was available at more than 90 per cent of US fuel stops, Ms Kiss said.

Loading...

Ethanol is perhaps the easiest biofuel to increase the use of, as it's already in the Australian market and it does not require the modifications that fuels like biodiesel do.

Ms Kiss said an education campaign about the benefits of ethanol-blended petrol, and a legislated mandate to make it more available, were what Australia needed to boost consumption.

The body representing sugarcane growers shared similar sentiments.

"An enforced ethanol mandate would build demand and therefore justify new investment in supply, which would underpin new diversified revenue streams for our industry," Canegrowers chief executive officer Dan Galligan said.

What are the downsides to biofuels?

Aside from the higher cost, some people have raised concerns about the environmental impact on land used to farm feedstock, and competition for agricultural land between food and fuel suppliers.

Australia has a small biofuels industry, and most of the output is exported. More than 70 per cent of our canola is exported to other countries, which crush and convert it to biofuels.

"Look, it's still way behind the rest of the world," said Mr Elia, from IFM Investors.

Highlights

Aviation fuel security plan focuses on refining, imports, and Supply chain resilience framework.

Sustainable aviation fuel development emerges as key long-term industry consideration area.

Fuel supply stability critical for aviation, freight logistics, and defence operations continuity.

A reported aviation fuel security plan could support Australia’s strategic future, drawing attention to the resilience of fuel supply chains. According to reports, the plan considers refining capacity, Import dependency, storage infrastructure, and the potential role of emerging fuel technologies. The debate continues around how to balance commercial viability with long-term national security priorities.

Importance of Aviation Fuel Security

Aviation fuel plays a critical role in enabling passenger travel, cargo transport, and emergency response services. According to reports, maintaining secure and reliable fuel availability is increasingly viewed as an essential part of national infrastructure planning. Disruptions in supply chains can have wide-ranging impacts across both economic and operational systems.

Refining Capacity and Import Dependency

Australia’s domestic refining capacity has declined over time, increasing reliance on imported fuel to meet Demand. According to reports, this dependency has placed greater emphasis on international supply chain stability and shipping logistics. Policy discussions continue around how to maintain adequate fuel availability while managing external risks and price Volatility.

Role of Sustainable Aviation Fuel

The debate continues around how Australia could develop domestic SAF production capability. According to reports, this includes considerations around feedstock availability, Investment requirements, and integration into existing aviation fuel systems.

Industry and Defence Alignment

Fuel security planning involves both commercial aviation and defence requirements. According to reports, coordination between government agencies, airlines, and defence Stakeholders is an important aspect of the policy framework. Ensuring continuity of supply is considered essential for national preparedness and operational resilience across sectors.

Risks

Heavy reliance on imports may expose supply chains to global disruptions.

High infrastructure costs could limit expansion of domestic fuel storage capacity.

Slow development of sustainable aviation fuel may delay emissions transition goals.

Geopolitical instability may impact fuel pricing and availability risks.

Summary

Australia’s aviation fuel security plan focuses on strengthening supply chain resilience through refining capacity, imports, storage, and sustainable aviation fuel development. The strategy reflects growing recognition of fuel’s importance for aviation, logistics, and defence.

While import reliance remains a key challenge, policy discussions continue around balancing commercial feasibility with long-term strategic and environmental objectives in the aviation sector.

text:
Vietnam demonstrated its clear commitment to become a serious SAF leader on Wednesday, as several key government ministries gathered in Da Nang for the country’s first international SAF summit and Asia SAF Association (ASAFA) signed two institutional agreements with state bodies.

The ASAFA Innovation & Policy Summit (IPS) Vietnam 2026, running 6–8 May in Da Nang, brought together leaders from approximately 70 organisations, including high-level policymakers from the National Assembly’s Committee for Economic and Financial Affairs, the Ministries of Industry and Trade, Finance, Construction, and Science and Technology, alongside airlines, fuel producers, financiers, and technology providers. The summit was opened by Mr. Ho Quang Buu, Vice Chairman of the Da Nang People’s Committee.

The first MOU was signed with the Agency for Innovation, Green Transition and Industry Promotion (IGIP), a body under Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade, establishing a strategic framework covering SAF capacity building, technical knowledge transfer, and policy development support. The second, signed with the Da Nang Innovation Startup Support Centre (DISSC), positions Da Nang as a hub for SAF innovation through co-organised events, expert networks and workforce development.

“Vietnam has the key fundamentals required to build a competitive SAF ecosystem,” said Fabrice Espinosa, Founder and CEO of ASAFA. “The question is not whether SAF will scale. The question is where, and who will lead.”

Since 2024, ASAFA has established itself as Asia-Pacific’s leading independent voice on SAF. Its members and partners, spanning 44 organisations across 17 countries, have shaped SAF policy across Asian governments, driven real SAF procurement and certificate purchases and produced the region’s first APAC SAF Outlook report. The association was recognised as winner of the EuroCham Sustainability Award 2025 and represented at COP30 in Belém.

IPS Vietnam 2026 is the first of three summits ASAFA will convene this year, with Thailand in June and Malaysia in October. Beyond the summits, ASAFA will release three major publications, launch a Market Structures Committee to harmonise regional standards, and open its first intake for the International SAF Professional Training Academy in September.
